title: Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz: A Dream Team at the US Open
summary:
Serena Williams, the 23-time Grand Slam singles champion, is making headlines again—this time teaming up with Carlos Alcaraz for the US Open mixed doubles. The pairing is a fascinating clash of eras: Williams won her first US Open mixed doubles title in 1998, five years before Alcaraz was even born.

Williams returned to tennis in June after a four-year hiatus, playing three doubles matches and a singles match at Wimbledon. Alcaraz, a seven-time major winner, has been sidelined for over four months with a wrist injury. Their combined 44 Grand Slam titles make them a formidable wildcard entry.

The US Open mixed doubles underwent a controversial revamp last year to attract more attention by including singles stars. The top six pairs by combined singles rankings receive direct entry, while eight others get wildcards. Defending champions Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori, the only doubles specialists with a main-draw wildcard, criticized the change as "profoundly wrong" but still won the title and $1 million.

The tournament runs from August 24-26, ending four days before the singles draw begins. The scoring system is shorter: four games win a set, no advantage scoring, and 10-point match tie-breaks instead of a third set.

Other notable pairings include Aryna Sabalenka with Novak Djokovic, Jessica Pegula with Taylor Fritz, and Iga Swiatek with Casper Ruud. Elina Svitolina will play with her husband Gael Monfils in his final Grand Slam before retirement.

As Williams steps back onto the court, fans are eager to see if this dream team can capture the title. The mixed doubles event has never been more star-studded—or more debated.
why_it_matters: The revamp shows how sports leagues sometimes change rules to boost viewership and star power, but those changes can frustrate traditionalists; the result may shape whether future Grand Slams treat doubles as a serious competition or a celebrity showcase.

background_read: Grand Slam tournaments such as the US Open (held annually in New York City) have traditionally treated mixed doubles as a sideshow, but officials have recently tried to attract singles stars with direct entries and wildcard invitations.
Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori (Italian doubles specialists) won the title under the revamped format, even as they criticized the new rules.
Serena Williams (a 23-time Grand Slam singles champion from the United States) returned to tennis this year after four years away, first appearing at Wimbledon in June.
Carlos Alcaraz (a seven-time major winner from Spain) has been out for over four months with a wrist injury, making this pairing a high-profile comeback story.

Mixed doubles often uses shorter scoring than regular matches, which can make results more unpredictable, and its prize and attention are still much smaller than singles; even so, star pairings such as this one have made the event far more visible and debated.

perspectives.description: Fans and organizers benefit from star-studded mixed doubles because well-known singles players attract larger crowds and media attention. The Williams-Alcaraz pairing brings together two generations of champions and could make mixed doubles feel more prestigious.

Doubles specialists like Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori see the new entry system as unfair because singles rankings determine many spots. Skilled doubles teams may be pushed aside for marketable singles stars who have less doubles experience.

The change reflects a broader sports pattern: events are often adjusted for television and ticket sales. Shorter scoring and wildcard entries may speed up matches, but they also shift mixed doubles away from its traditional tests of doubles skill.

If the star pairings perform well, the US Open may keep or expand the revamped format. If injuries or early exits occur, officials might face more pressure from specialists to revise wildcard and entry rules again.
